**Question #1 - Why program synthesis (of neural programs) as the target domain?**

Thank you for raising this. Our view is aligned with yours: many domains can be framed as parameterized learning, and our method is not intrinsically tied to program synthesis. We chose program synthesis as the testbed for three reasons.

**(1) Program synthesis is general enough to subsume many other domains.**

 Many settings can be cast as “synthesize a program given a parameterized intent”:

1) Task-incremental continual learning → program synthesis over a task-ID–conditioned family;


2) Program-by-example (PBE) → intent given by a small set of I/O examples;


3) Natural-language control → intent given by an NL description of the desired behavior.


In this sense, program synthesis is not a narrow niche but a general umbrella: other domains can be phrased as program synthesis with different forms of (U). 

**(2) It provides the cleanest setting to establish feasibility.**

 We deliberately adopt a **full-information** setup in which the user intent (U) contains all the information needed to specify the program within a fixed family. This makes our setting the natural “easy end” of an intent spectrum and is by design: in this first cornerstone paper, our goal is to cleanly establish **feasibility** of strict zero-shot $U \mapsto \theta$ and to keep the learned neural programs interpretable. 

In many other domains (as noted in (1)), the intent signal U is **partial** or **noisy** rather than fully specifying the program. Typical cases include:

1) a task ID that only indicates a coarse sub-task type,

2) a small set of I/O examples (PBE), or

3) a natural-language instruction that under-specifies the desired behaviour.

This gives a spectrum from full-information U (our setting) to increasingly weaker signals (PBE, task-ID conditioning, NL instructions). Since the notion of a neural program is still new, and synthesizing an entire weight set in a single forward pass is generally viewed as ambitious (most hypernetworks generate layer-by-layer), we focus first on showing that the full-information case is both feasible and interpretable. We then explicitly position PBE and natural-language intents—where U is no longer fully informative—as natural next steps in our Future Work.

**(3) Program structure supports subprograms and compositionality.**

 Programs come with a natural notion of subroutines, and this is useful for interpretation. In our setting, the mechanistic analysis of ADDMOD-p shows that the synthesized networks admit a clear **subgraph = subprogram** structure. Two design choices make this possible: the hypernetwork is **permutation-invariant**, and **end-to-end training** encourages it to reuse as much of the target network’s weights—and thus its sub-neural-circuits—as possible.
As a result, the synthesized Transformer separates cleanly into functional components. In ADDMOD-p:

• $(W_E)$ and $(W_U)$ implement the part of the program that depends on $(p)$, mapping the intent to a latent angle;


• the middle layers remain largely invariant across (p) because they implement the shared subroutine—*addition in cosine space*, which is itself agnostic to the specific angle.


This kind of localized, mechanistic decomposition is far harder to obtain in less structured domains.

Thank you for the careful and positive review. Your comments accurately capture the paper’s main goals, and we respond below to your specific weaknesses and questions.

**Weakness #1 — “Benefits of structure-awareness supported only by theory; lacking ablations to isolate Meta-GNN components”**

We appreciate this point and agree that isolating architectural factors is important. Our framework already embeds a coarse ablation of structure-awareness via the three meta-learners: Meta-MLP has no structural grouping, Meta-gMLP adds group-tied initialization, and Meta-GNN further introduces graph connectivity, message passing, and permutation handling. This progressive sequence explains the monotonic gains in Tables 2–3 as we add structure, rather than just capacity.

In addition, in early experiments (on a smaller Meta-GNN for faster sweeps), we explicitly ablated key Meta-GNN design choices:

**init_mode** ∈ {all, per_group, global}: per-node, per-group, or globally shared initial embeddings;

**aggr** ∈ {attn, avg, sum} with **use_norm** ∈ {True, False}: the aggregation method for messages;

**bidirectional** ∈ {True, False}: whether to include reverse edges in message passing;

**rev_edge_mode** ∈ {shared, separate, --}: for bidirectional graphs, shared ties forward and reverse edges to the same embedding, while separate gives reverse edges their own parameters; -- denotes the unidirectional case (no reverse edges at all).


The table below reports best query accuracy across these configurations on ADDMOD-p:
| init_mode  | aggr | use_norm | bidirectional | rev_edge_mode | best_test_qry_acc      |
|-----------|------|----------|---------------|---------------|------------------------|
| all       | attn | False    | True          | shared        | 0.964 $\pm$ 0.016      |
| per_group | attn | False    | True          | shared        | 0.976 $\pm$ 0.029      |
| global    | attn | False    | True          | shared        | 0.969 $\pm$ 0.021      |
|-----------|------|----------|---------------|---------------|------------------------|
| per_group | avg  | False    | True          | shared        | 0.949 $\pm$ 0.032      |
| per_group | avg  | True     | True          | shared        | 0.964 $\pm$ 0.013      |
| per_group | sum  | False    | True          | shared        | 0.947 $\pm$ 0.015      |
| per_group | sum  | True     | True          | shared        | 0.954 $\pm$ 0.012      |
|-----------|------|----------|---------------|---------------|------------------------|
| per_group | attn | False    | False         | --            | 0.965 $\pm$ 0.023      |
| per_group | attn | False    | True          | separate      | **0.979 $\pm$ 0.014**      |

Overall, the differences are modest: all configurations achieve strong performance (best_test_qry_acc typically in the 0.95–0.98 range). We therefore selected our final Meta-GNN configuration by varying one factor at a time: 

(i) we first chose init_mode = per_group, which attains the best performance in this sweep while also scaling more parameter-efficiently than all for larger target networks; 

(ii) conditioned on that, we compared aggregators and found attn to outperform or match avg/sum (with or without normalization); and 

(iii) with per_group + attn fixed, enabling bidirectional message passing and using separate parameters for reverse edges (rev_edge_mode = separate) yields the best performance. 

Note these ablations were run with a smaller Meta-GNN (<50k meta-parameters) for efficiency, so the absolute numbers can be slightly higher than in the main paper, where Meta-GNN is scaled up to ~200k parameters to match other baselines under the same training budget (making the larger model relatively under-trained).

We will add this ablation table and discussion to the appendix (see new Appendix §C.3) . If the paper is accepted, we plan to extend the same Meta-GNN component ablations to the other two datasets (SumFirst-n and 1D-ARC) to provide further empirical insight into which structural choices matter most across domains.

**Weakness #3 — “Related work section appears to be lacking”**

We focused the original Related Work on the foundational HyperNetworks and MAML papers because most subsequent hypernetwork/meta-learning work adopts essentially the same setting: *fast adaptation* from task data or **test I/O**, often with layer-wise weight generation. This is fundamentally **different** from our setting of strict *zero-shot* synthesis **from user intent**, generating the **entire weight vector** with **out-of-distribution generalization**. For that reason, we believed citing the seminal works was sufficient to delineate the gap.

To help readers situate our contribution in the broader landscape, we will also briefly mention a few representative later works and explicitly contrast their regime with ours, for example:

1. Task-conditioned hypernetworks / continual learning:

     von Oswald et al., “Continual Learning with Hypernetworks,” ICLR 2020. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00695)


2. Hypernets as meta-learners:

     Zhao et al., “Meta-Learning via Hypernetworks,” MetaLearn 2020 (NeurIPS Workshop). (https://doi.org/10.3929/ethz-b-000465883)


3. Hypernetworks at larger scale:

     Beck et al., “Recurrent Hypernetworks are Surprisingly Strong in Meta-RL,” NeurIPS 2023. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14970)


4. Hypernetwork-based meta-learning for scientific ML:

     Cho et al., “Hypernetwork-based Meta-Learning for Low-Rank Physics-Informed Neural Networks,” NeurIPS 2023. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09528)



Again, all of these works assume task data at test time and typically generate weights layer-by-layer; none address the zero-shot, full-weight, out-of-distribution synthesis setting we study, which is why our approach is complementary rather than incremental to this line. We will clarify this distinction and add these citations in the revised Related Work section.

Thank you again for the thoughtful review and for updating your score — we really appreciate your engagement with the paper.

We have now uploaded a revised version that incorporates the changes discussed in our author response, including a Scope & Limitations section, an expanded Related Work and contributions discussion, and additional appendix material (e.g., Meta-GNN component ablations). Newly added or substantially revised passages are marked in blue in the PDF for ease of review.

If you have a chance to look at the updated version and feel there are still parts of the presentation that would benefit from another iteration, we’d be grateful for any brief pointers (e.g., specific sections or arguments). We’re happy to refine further where needed.

summary.value:
The paper considers the problem of program synthesis. The authors refer to a neural network that approximates a symbolic program as a “neural program” (“NeuroP”) and explore whether a hypernetwork can be effective at converting a program specification (given by “user intent”) into a neural program. They note that a neural program has many neuron-permutation symmetries that can hinder a hypernetwork’s performance. To address this, the neural program’s structure is represented as a graph, that is divided into weight subsets. The hypernetwork then outputs a neural program in 3 steps: 1) A subset-specific encoder transforms the user intent to a corresponding latent vector. 2) The graph structure is utilized, along with message passing, in order to ensure the permutation equivariance inside the necessary weight subsets. 3) A subset-specific decoder is used to generate the weights of a neural program.

The paper claims three contributions: establishing NeuroP as an alternative to symbolic program synthesis; providing empirical evidence that using structure-aware hypernetworks can lead to strong OOD generalization across diverse program families; releasing the code and datasets.

Appears to provide a novel approach (in the program synthesis literature) to generating neural programs using a hypernetwork.

Provide an interesting comparison between the performance of group-aware and group-and-structure aware hypernetworks.

Their experiments cover an MLP as well as the transformer architecture, demonstrating that the method is effective for both.

Thank you for the detailed review and the many helpful suggestions. Below I respond to each point in turn and note the corresponding manuscript changes.

**Weakness #1 — “Limited evaluation – experiments and baselines”**

**Why not include more “neural program synthesis” baselines?**
 To the best of our knowledge—and consistent with the other reviewers’ assessments—the program-synthesis literature does not yet contain a method that treats the weight vector itself as the program (neural program). In that sense, our work is the first to articulate this modality formally and to provide feasibility and empirical evidence that such a continuous relaxation is learnable and yields clear generalization gains.
We have clarified these distinctions in the revised Related Work (§2) and Limitations (§6).

**Weakness #2 — “Limited novelty; contributions not clearly supported”**

Our approach is **novel** in both **program synthesis** (treating weights-as-programs with out-of-distribution generalization) and **hypernetworks** (a permutation-aware graph hypernetwork that generates all weights in one shot). The core difficulty we tackle is **strict zero-shot out-of-parameter generalization**: given an unseen program parameter, the hypernetwork must synthesize a full weight vector $\theta$ that works for all inputs of that program. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to achieve near-perfect accuracy in this regime and to provide a mechanistic explanation of why this generalization occurs.

*“Introducing the concept of a neural program is not a contribution.”*

 For Contribution #1, our intent is not to claim novelty for terminology alone, but for the formalization of neural programs as a continuous program modality and the accompanying result: that this relaxation makes the synthesis problem **learnable**. Beyond defining the modality, we show that a meta-learner can reliably map from user intent to model weights, producing executable programs in one forward pass with **strong generalization**.

*“The second listed contribution … is not supported by the limited evaluation.”*

Our claims for this contribution are: (1) intent-to-weight synthesis is feasible, and (2) structure-aware meta-learners achieve strong OOD generalization across diverse program families. We believe the current empirical evidence supports both the feasibility and generalization claims:

(1. feasibility) All three meta-learners synthesize full parameter sets (across two architectures, up to ~17k weights) in a single forward pass, and achieve ≈100% in-distribution accuracy (Table 2).


(2. OOD generalization) OOD accuracy is consistently high—typically 80–95%—across multiple program families with unseen intents.


To explain why this generalization occurs, we include a mechanistic analysis on ADDMOD-p: Meta-GNN recovers the canonical clock circuit and admits a closed-form map $(p\mapsto(W_E(p),W_U(p)))$. This goes beyond reporting numbers and directly inspects the synthesized mechanism.


If there is a particular aspect of the feasibility or OOD claim that you feel is not sufficiently supported, could you point us to it? We would be happy to clarify or expand on it in the revision.

*“It is possible that the way the hypernetwork is constructed is novel, but if so it should be explicitly states as a contribution.”*

We agree that the architectural novelty should be explicit. Our main contribution on the hypernetwork side is a generative, permutation-aware graph hypernetwork that:

1) represents the entire target network as a neural graph (nodes = biases, edges = weights);

2) ties encoders/decoders across permutation-equivalent neurons and edges, enforcing the correct symmetry; and

3) generates the full weight vector in a single forward pass, rather than layer-by-layer as in prior hypernetworks.

We will make this explicit in the contribution statement.

Thank you for the review and for taking the time to engage with the paper. We address your concern below.

**Weakness #1 — “The tasks are illustrative but rather simple without significant practical usage”**

Although the program families have simple symbolic descriptions, the learning problem we study is not: we require strict **zero-shot out-of-parameter generalization**, where the hypernetwork must synthesize a full weight vector $\theta$ that works for **unseen** program parameters. To the best of our knowledge, no existing method in program synthesis, meta-learning, or hypernetworks can do this, and our capacity-matched direct baselines also fail. The benchmarks are therefore intentionally minimal in surface form so that this **hard generalization** target can be isolated and the **learned mechanism** can be inspected, before moving to larger and less interpretable domains.

**Mechanism before scale.**

 The key research question of this paper is conceptual: *can a meta-learner discover a consistent mapping from user intent U to weights $\theta$ that yields a valid executable network in one forward pass?*

 Establishing this required controlled families with known ground-truth structure (e.g., the “clock” algorithm in ADDMOD-p). These tasks provide interpretable validation that the model recovers the intended computation—something that would be impossible to verify in larger, noisy domains.

Furthermore, the mechanistic analysis of ADDMOD-p yields a clear **subgraph = subprogram** view: for instance, $(W_E)$ and $(W_U)$ encode the mapping from $(U)$ to the latent angle, while the middle layers implement addition in cosine space. This decomposition is only possible because the meta-learner is (i) **permutation-invariant**, ensuring consistent treatment of symmetric units, and (ii) trained **end-to-end**, which encourages the hypernetwork to reuse sub-neural-circuits across tasks. 

**Hidden complexity in weight space**

 Although their symbolic form may be short (except for 1D-ARC), these tasks are far from trivial in the neural representation:

1) Each target program corresponds to a point in a continuous parameter space of dimension $10^2$ - $10^5$


2) The meta-learner must discover smooth functional structure across this high-dimensional space, without discrete search or any hand-crafted DSL.

 Empirically, direct training on these tasks fails to generalize, while our structure-aware Meta-GNN succeeds—confirming that the challenge lies in weight-space generalization, not symbolic length.

**Foundation for richer domains (incl. ARC-AGI).**

We view these benchmarks as controlled proofs-of-concept before scaling to realistic domains where “intent” is more complex (e.g., multi-variable specifications, program-by-example tasks, or natural-language prompts). In particular, 1D-ARC is a 1D variant of the ARC-AGI benchmark—a real, program-by-example task where state-of-the-art LLMs still struggle. Our intent→weights framework extends naturally to the full ARC-AGI PBE setting (using the example set as U), and we now explicitly identify this as a key direction in the Limitations and Future Work sections.

In summary, this trajectory parallels the historical path of symbolic synthesis systems, which first validated search strategies on arithmetic and list-processing tasks before extending to spreadsheet coding or algorithmic reasoning. We have clarified this trajectory in the revised Limitations and Future Work sections.

**Question #2 — “Meta-GNN does not achieve the best generalization across all tasks—what explains these cases?”**

We appreciate this careful reading of Tables 2–3; below we provide intuition for the few cases where Meta-GNN is not numerically best and explain how they fit our overall view of search space and OOD difficulty.

**(1) ADDMOD-p (Table 2): near-tie due to a small effective search space.**

 Meta-GNN (0.943) is a very close second to Meta-MLP (0.947). A useful way to view difficulty is via the effective search space:

$ \text{SearchSpace} \approx |\Pi| \times |\mathrm{Sol}|,$

where $(|\Pi|)$ counts neuron-permutation symmetries of the target template and $(|\mathrm{Sol}|)$ is the number of functionally distinct neural realizations of the task. For ADDMOD-p, prior work indicates a **single canonical “clock” mechanism**, so $(|\mathrm{Sol}|\approx 1)$. Then:

• Meta-MLP effectively explores $(|\Pi|\times 1)$;


• Meta-GNN, by enforcing permutation structure, reduces permutations to a much smaller $(|\Pi_{\text{sub}}|\ll |\Pi|)$ and thus explores $(|\Pi_{\text{sub}}|\times 1)$.


Because $(|\mathrm{Sol}|)$ is ~1, collapsing permutations yields only a modest relative advantage—hence the near-tie. In regimes where $(|\mathrm{Sol}|>1)$ (many valid neural realizations), the gap widens: Meta-GNN simultaneously shrinks the permutation factor and stabilizes selection among multiple solutions, providing larger gains.

**(2) 1D-ARC families (Table 3): OOD severity and training horizon matter.**

• **OOD definition differs by family.** For Fill/Flip/Hollow, the “OOD” split uses the same hyperparameter seen in training; MoveRight and RecolorBar hold out true task parameters (unseen distances/colors), yielding stricter OOD.


• **Direct Transformer overfits; meta methods keep improving OOD.** On families with milder OOD, the direct model can overfit early while meta models continue to improve. We will add training curves in the appendix to showcase this; e.g., for *Hollow*, Meta-GNN trails at the reported epoch but its loss is still decreasing—suggesting longer training would close the gap.


• **When solution multiplicity is high, symmetry helps more.** On *Flip*, Meta-GNN leads. This matches the search-space view in (1): when $(|\mathrm{Sol}|)$ is large (many neural realizations of the same transformation), reducing the permutation factor with Meta-GNN shrinks the effective search space more substantially, so the gain over Meta-MLP/Meta-gMLP is large.



**Question #3 — “Does the structure-aware design offer additional advantages (size, efficiency)?”**

Yes. The shared encoders/decoders and tied parameters substantially reduce trainable size—Meta-GNN has fewer trainable parameters than a naive fully-connected hypernetwork of similar capacity—and its message-passing operations scale with the sparsity of the neural graph rather than total weights. We have added a brief paragraph quantifying this in Appendix C.

summary.value: This paper is in the field of hypernetworks. Given a user intent, it generate specific weights for another (target) neural network to complete the task. The main contribution is that the proposed architecture considered neuron-permutation symmetry (that is, for example, the order of neurons in a layer does not influence the functionality of the network). The architecture of the target network is transformed to a graph in which nodes are biases and edges are weights. While swapable nodes/edges are assigned different positional encodings to differentiate them, they are processed by the same encode function. $K$ message-passing processes are done on the graph, which include a permutation-invariant aggregation to merge all the informations from neighbors. Finally, every node and edge obtains an embedding which is then decoded as a scalar.

- A mechanistic analysis is provided, which shows strong evidence that the proposed architecture learns a generalizable solution

comment.value:
**Weakness #2 — “Each task uses only one shallow target network configuration…”**

We agree this is an important limitation, and below we explain why we deliberately started from simple target network architectures, how this choice supports our mechanistic analysis.

**(1) Step-1 focus on feasibility.**

 This paper’s goal is to establish that strict **zero-shot** synthesis from user intent to weights is feasible and benefits from permutation-aware structure. We therefore fixed compact target templates to control confounds and will extend to deeper/heterogeneous targets in follow-up work (noted in §6 Limitations/§7 Conclusion).


**(2) Interpretability to verify mechanism.**

 Prior work on 1-layer Transformers for ADDMOD-p identifies a canonical clock mechanism, giving a known reference. In this setting, our mechanistic analysis shows a **subgraph = subprogram** decomposition: $((W_E, W_U))$ encode the intent $(U=p)$ as a latent angle, and the middle block performs addition in cosine space. This verification—confirming how generalization occurs—would be substantially harder to obtain in deeper/noisier stacks. We’d like to highlight again, two design choices help make it observable: (i) **permutation-invariance** through Graph Hypernetwork; and (ii) **end-to-end training** (encourages reuse of sub-circuits across intents).


Finally, it’s worth mention that Meta-GNN scales linearly with the node/edge count of the target’s neural graph; moving to multi-block Transformers or CNN stages corresponds to enlarging that graph rather than changing the synthesis principle. We have clarified this scaling path in §C.4 and outlined deeper/heterogeneous targets as next steps.

**Weakness #3 — “Lack of direct empirical comparisons with traditional (neuro-symbolic) synthesis methods”**

We share your interest in such comparisons, and we clarify below why truly apples-to-apples experiments with classical and neuro-symbolic systems are nontrivial in our DSL-free setting, and how we therefore position our work relative to them.

**(1) Apples-to-apples requires a DSL, which undercuts our aim.**

 A core advantage of our neural program view is that it is **DSL-free**: the program is the weight vector itself. Classical search-based synthesizers (e.g., SyGuS) and neuro-symbolic systems operate over a hand-crafted DSL. To run such baselines here, we would first need to invent a bespoke DSL; the resulting performance would largely reflect the DSL’s coverage/inductive bias rather than the synthesis mechanism. This would obscure the central question we study: *is continuous intent→weights synthesis feasible and beneficial in weight space?* We have clarified this rationale in Related Work (§2) and Limitations (§6).

**(2) Direct neural baselines expose a core deficiency.**

 Although these families appear simple symbolically, they are non-trivial in weight space. Our capacity-matched direct baselines—standard over-parameterized MLPs or Transformers trained end-to-end on $((U,X) \to Y)$—fail to **OOD-generalize** to unseen intents, whereas the structure-aware graph hypernetwork, which receives exactly the same information $((U, X))$, succeeds. While not a direct comparison to neuro-symbolic systems, this contrast reveals a fundamental limitation of current fully neural approaches and underscores the advantage of our intent→weights synthesis paradigm.

**Question #1 — “What other tasks are common in traditional synthesis, and could this method be compared directly?”**

Please see **Weakness #3** for why we avoid direct comparisons (DSL mismatch). This paper is step-1: feasibility—a proof of concept that strict zero-shot intent→weights synthesis works under the simplest intent model, where $(U)$ fully specifies the task within a fixed program space.
A natural next step is to relax this and treat $(U)$ as **partial/noisy** intent:

1) Program-by-example (PBE): encode a few I/O pairs $((X,Y))$ as the intent signal, synthesizing $(\theta)$ from a small support set (e.g., spreadsheet/FlashFill-style transformations).


2) Natural-language instructions: parse NL prompts as noisy, under-specified intents and condition the hypernetwork accordingly.


We note these directions in new §6 Limitations and §7 Conclusion.

summary.value: Traditional program synthesis methods that search within a template space rely heavily on handcrafted templates and incur substantial computational costs as template size increases. To bridge these gaps, the authors introduce the lens of meta-learning with hypernetworks, defining a neural program (NeuroP) as a differentiable program modality that enables continuous, gradient-based optimization. The authors then propose Meta-GNN, a structure-aware hypernetwork capable of generating the complete set of weights for a target architecture given a user intent U. Experimental results show that Meta-GNN demonstrates strong out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization compared to all baselines. It is notable that on the ADDMOD-p task, Meta-GNN learns a canonical clock representation, indicating that it captures underlying, generalizable computational regularities.

strengths.value:
1. The proposed method makes meaningful contributions across multiple prior research directions and demonstrates clear originality:

   - Leveraging hypernetworks for program synthesis is an innovative idea that mitigates the dependence on handcrafted DSLs present in neuro-symbolic approaches.

   - The proposed Meta-GNN employs message passing and group-tied encoders and decoders to address the permutation symmetry problem in traditional hypernetworks.

   - Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is a critical challenge in both meta-learning and hypernetwork research, and the paper shows that Meta-GNN achieves strong OOD generalization performance.

2. The paper is well-structured and comprehensive, with clear formal definitions and thorough explanations of the key design components of Meta-GNN.

weaknesses.value:
1. The claimed benefits of structure-awareness in improving generalization and performance are supported only by theoretical explaination, lacking ablation studies. Specifically, while the selected baselines partially demonstrate that greater structure-awareness correlates with better generalization, Meta-GNN, as a graph neural network, differs topologically from the MLP-based baselines. It would be valuable to further investigate the contribution of Meta-GNN’s own components.
  
2. In the experimental section, each task domain employs only a single target network configuration. As shown in Table 1, all target networks are shallow (mostly one-layer) , which limits evidence for scalability and cross-architecture generalization.
  
3. The paper lacks direct empirical comparisons with traditional methods, such as neuro-symbolic baselines, which would strengthen the claim of superiority over existing approaches.

questions.value:
1. What other tasks are commonly studied in traditional program synthesis, and could this method be compared directly with classical or symbolic approaches on those tasks?
  
2. In Tables 2 and 3, Meta-GNN does not achieve the best generalization across all tasks. What might explain these cases?
  
3. Beyond demonstrating strong OOD generalization, does the structure-aware design offer additional advantages, such as smaller model size, reduced training cost, or improved efficiency?
